content: The Giant Puffball, scientifically known as Calvatia gigantea, is a type of puffball mushroom that is commonly found in meadows, fields, and deciduous forests across the globe. It typically appears during late summer and autumn. Most specimens of the Giant Puffball grow to a diameter of 10 to 70 cm, although some exceptional examples can reach diameters of up to 150 cm and weigh as much as 20 kg. The interior of a mature Giant Puffball is greenish-brown, while the inside of an immature puffball is white. These large, white mushrooms are edible when they are young. However, this information alone is insufficient to reliably distinguish Giant Puffballs from other potentially poisonous species, such as Scleroderma areolatum. Therefore, this description should not be used as a definitive guide to determine whether a mushroom is safe to eat. Some individuals claim that the cooked flesh of the Giant Puffball has a taste similar to tofu. When preparing the mushroom for consumption, it is important to remove any brown portions and tough skin, if present. The mushroom should not be soaked in water. Puffballs can be sautéed, broiled, or breaded and fried. They do not dehydrate well but can be cooked and then frozen for later use. All members of the true puffball family are considered edible, but it is crucial to cut open young specimens to ensure there are no gills inside. The presence of gills would indicate that the mushroom is not a puffball and could potentially be a toxic species. For example, deadly Amanitas have a volva or universal veil that completely envelops the young mushrooms. Before emerging from the volva, these mushrooms can resemble small, round puffballs. Additionally, puffballs can be mistaken for earthballs (Scleroderma citrinum), which are characterized by a much firmer, elastic fruiting body and an interior that turns dark purplish-black with white reticulations early in development. The fruiting body of a puffball mushroom develops over a few weeks and then begins to decompose and rot. At this stage, it should not be consumed. Unlike most mushrooms, all the spores of the Giant Puffball are produced inside the fruiting body. Large specimens can contain several trillion spores. These spores are yellowish, smooth, and measure 3 to 5 micrometers in size. Interestingly, the dry spores can be used as a coagulant to help stop bleeding. The classification of the Giant Puffball has undergone revisions in recent years. The previously recognized class Gasteromycetes, which included all puffballs, has been found to be polyphyletic. Some taxonomists now place the Giant Puffball and other members of the genus Calvatia in the order Agaricales. Historically, this species has also been classified under two other genera, Lycoperdon and Langermannia. When Giant Puffballs reach the stage where they release spores, they become toxic and should not be consumed. Images of Giant Puffballs at this spore-releasing stage show their transformation into a state unsuitable for ingestion.
